# Improving sampling: fixing an over-specified model

Sometimes the chains misbehave. We might see high R-hat values, tiny ESS and trace plots that wander and drift apart. Our first intution is often that "the sampler is broken", but far more often the model is asking the data to estimate something it **cannot**. This is an *over-specified* model, and the cure is to look at how you are building the model and the priors, not to try and fix the algorithm.

::: callout-tip
The Folk Theorem of Statistical Computing (Gelman 2008): "When you have computational problems, often there’s a problem with your model. "
:::

## The data

We use `random-effects.csv`. This is benthic-cover survey from the same Kia Province reefs you met with the fish counts. Each row is one transect, and `cover` is the per-cent cover of branching *Acropora* coral. There are several transects per site, so `site` is a natural grouping variable for random effects.

## A broken model

Here is a model that tries to give every site its own free mean, on top of a global intercept, with very diffuse priors:

```
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    cover[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha + beta[site[i]]
  }
  alpha ~ dnorm(0, 1000)
  for (j in 1:J) {
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 1000)
  }
}
```

Set `J` to the number of sites (20) alongside `N` in the constants, then fit it. The diagnostics will be dreadful. You will notice the trace plots drift and wander and different chains don't converge on the same distribution (tick the 'show array parameters' button if you want to see traces for each `beta`).  R-hat for `alpha` and the `beta[j]` will be huge, and ESS be in the single digits.


## Non-identifiability

Non-identifiability is a common problem, but it's not always that obvious. Here's a really obvious example to start you off. 

Consider the linear predictor: $\log(\lambda_i) = \alpha + \beta_{\text{site}[i]}$. You can add any constant $c$ to $\alpha$ and subtract the same $c$ from *every* $\beta_j$, and the predictions are completely unchanged:

$$
(\alpha + c) + (\beta_j - c) = \alpha + \beta_j
$$

So the data can nail each sum $\alpha + \beta_j$, but never $\alpha$ and the $\beta_j$ separately — there are infinitely many equally good answers along a ridge. The two diffuse `dnorm(0, 1000)` priors do nothing to break the tie, so the sampler slides up and down that ridge forever. That is what a high R-hat and tiny ESS are telling you.

## Fix 1: partial pooling and sensible priors

Back to our model of reefs. Make the site effects deviations around the global mean, drawn from a shared distribution whose width $\sigma_b$ the model estimates. Anchoring them at zero identifies $\alpha$ as the grand mean, and the shared prior pools information across sites:

```
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    cover[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha + b[site[i]]
  }
  for (j in 1:J) {
    b[j] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
  }
  alpha   ~ dnorm(0, 10)
  sigma.b ~ dunif(0, 10)
}
```

Don't forget to re-enter J=20 before running the model. 

Two changes fixed our issue:

1. **Identifiability** — the `b[j]` are centred on 0 with a shared, estimated SD, so they can no longer trade off freely against `alpha`.
2. **Sensible priors** — `dnorm(0, 10)` on the log-scale intercept and a bounded `dunif(0, 10)` on $\sigma_b$ are weakly informative rather than absurdly wide.

Refit and watch R-hat collapse from the tens to close to 1.0, and ESS climb from single digits into the hundreds. (It will not land exactly on 1.0 for every parameter on this dataset — see the note at the end of the module for why.)

## Fix 2: Reparameterisation

In hierarchical models the group SD $\sigma_b$ and the group effects $b_j$ are strongly coupled, creating a funnel-shaped posterior that is hard to sample (the "centred" parameterisation). A **non-centred** form decouples them:

```
for (j in 1:J) {
  z[j] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  b[j] <- sigma.b * z[j]
}
```

This is the same model, it just has a much friendlier geometry for the sampling algorithm.

## A sampler that helps (but is not a fix)

The two fixes above are about the **model**. There's also a setting that changes
how FANGS *samples* whatever model you give it: **Sampler engine**, in the
sampler settings.

- **Standard** updates one parameter at a time. It works for any model FANGS can
  parse, which is why it's the default.
- **Blocked** updates all the fixed coefficients together, and all the group
  effects at once, and it makes moves that shift $\alpha$ up while shifting
  every $\beta_j$ down by the same amount — travelling *along* the ridge from
  the section above instead of crawling across it. It applies to GLMMs: a
  normal, Poisson or binomial response with `dnorm` priors on the coefficients.

Use **Blocked** whenever you're fitting a mixed-effects model, and especially
with many groups or more than a few hundred rows. On the 50-row example dataset
it runs about 100× faster, and the gain in *accuracy per second* is larger still
— because of the $\alpha$ ↔ $\beta_j$ ridge the standard engine needs roughly
900× more time to pin the intercept down as precisely.

Two things to be clear about:

- It targets the **same posterior**. This is a speed and mixing improvement, not
  a different model, and not a different answer.
- It **does not rescue an over-specified model.** A genuinely non-identifiable
  model still has bad R-hat and ESS on either engine, because the problem is in
  the model, not the algorithm. Fix the model first (Fixes 1 and 2); then pick
  the engine.

If your model isn't one the blocked engine supports, FANGS quietly falls back to
Standard and tells you so in the status bar.

## Fix 3: A sum-to-zero constraint

Fix 1 identified $\alpha$ by giving the $b_j$ a shared prior centred on zero. That works because the prior pulls the group effects toward zero, which stops them drifting off together. But it is a *soft* constraint — the $b_j$ are only centred on zero **on average, in the prior**, and nothing stops a particular draw from having them all positive, with $\alpha$ shifted down to compensate.

With a good number of groups that is usually enough — twenty site effects average out and the ridge is effectively closed. With **few** groups it is often not. There is little information about $\sigma_b$, so the chains can follow the prior out to large values, and the $\alpha$-versus-$b_j$ ridge reopens — exactly the problem from the start of this module, just narrower.

You can close it completely by making the constraint **hard**: let all but one group effect be free, and define the last as minus the sum of the others.

Here it is for a model with four groups:

```
b[1] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
b[2] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
b[3] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
b[4] <- -(b[1] + b[2] + b[3])
```

Now the four offsets sum to exactly zero in **every** draw, not just on average. There is no longer any direction the chains can slide along, so $\alpha$ is pinned down as the unambiguous grand mean across groups. A $J$-group model needs $J-1$ free effects and one deterministic line — which is why this is a tool for a handful of groups rather than twenty.

::: callout-note
## Why not always do this?

The sum-to-zero constraint costs you something: the last group effect is no longer a stochastic node, so it has no prior of its own and is not shrunk in the same way as the others. With a decent number of groups the soft constraint of Fix 1 is simpler, scales without writing a line per group, and pools information more even-handedly.

Reach for Fix 3 when you have **few groups** — a handful of experimental blocks, say — and the intercept will not converge despite a sensible prior on $\sigma_b$. That is precisely the situation in the summative challenge (Module 21), where four blocks give R-hat above 5 for $\alpha$ with free effects, and 1.01 with the constraint. Same data, same priors, same posterior means — only the parameterisation differs.
:::

## Your task

1. Fit the **broken** model and read the worst R-hat and minimum ESS from the **Summary** tab.
2. Fix it with the partial-pooling version above (adjust priors if you like).
3. Refit and record the **before/after** worst R-hat and minimum ESS in the table below.
4. **Optional:** try Fix 2 (non-centred) as an extra row in the table and compare.

::: callout-note
## Do not expect perfect diagnostics here

Fix 1 is a huge improvement on this dataset — the worst R-hat drops from the
**thirties** to roughly **1.4** with long enough chains (4 chains x 4000, burn-in
2000) — but it does not reach 1.0, and that is worth understanding rather than
papering over. At the default sampler settings it is worse still and varies a lot
between runs, which is itself a sign the chains have not settled.

Five of the twenty sites have **zero** coral cover on every transect. Their $b_j$
are held finite by the shared prior and individually converge well (R-hat ≈ 1.03),
but they sit far below the others, around $-3.3$. To accommodate that spread the
model inflates $\sigma_b$ to about 3, which **widens the $\alpha$-versus-$b_j$
ridge** — so $\alpha$ ends up the worst-mixing parameter in the model
(R-hat ≈ 1.5), not the zero sites themselves.

The lesson is the Folk Theorem again: the stubborn diagnostics are pointing at a
modelling problem, which here is the likelihood. A response that is 43% zeros
wants a zero-inflated or negative-binomial model, not a plain Poisson. Fixing the
parameterisation can only take you so far when the distribution is wrong.
:::
